new_statements.quote: El acento se da con la forma básica de la construcción gramatical, que consiste de una raíz simple o de una raíz más un sufijo de voz (véase Sec. 3.3.1.3). Las formas monosilábicas siempre son acentuadas. Sean de vocal simple o diptongo, son de la misma duración, pues la vocal simple se da con un alargamiento fonético y un tono descendente. [...] Las formas bisilábicas llevan el acento en la segunda sílaba. [...] Las formas trisilábicas también llevan el acento en la segunda sílaba. [...] Cuando se añaden sufijos a la forma básica, las sílabas alternas llevan el acento.
new_statements.translation: Stress goes with the basic form of the grammatical construction, which consists of a simple root or of a root plus a voice suffix (see Sec. 3.3.1.3). Monosyllabic forms are always stressed. Whether they have a simple vowel or a diphthong they have the same duration, since the simple vowel occurs with phonetic lengthening and a falling tone. [...] Disyllabic forms carry the stress on the second syllable. [...] Trisyllabic forms also carry the stress on the second syllable. [...] When suffixes are added to the basic form, alternate syllables carry the stress.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has a Secoya entry with an empty rule field and no existing stress statements, so nothing to agree or disagree with; this work supplies the placement: stress on the second syllable of the basic form (root or root+voice suffix), monosyllables always stressed, alternating stress on added suffixes. Opened from archive.org (Rosetta Project scans of the same 1990 Quito edition, title page and ToC confirmed) because the listed open_url on sil.org returned a not reachable by automated download challenge on both attempts; only chapter 2 (sections 2.1-2.5.5) plus ToC, sec. 1.1-1.2 and sec. 2.6 were available as scans, not the complete 113-page volume.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is assigned to the 'basic form' (root, or root plus voice suffix): monosyllabic roots are always stressed (realised with lengthening and falling pitch), and disyllabic and trisyllabic basic forms are stressed on their second syllable (examples /kuhí/ 'tooth', /maʔá/ 'path', /tití/ 'arrive'; /ʔapási/ 'zapote', /mɨsádu/ 'you pl.', /sɨsɨ́ko/ 'squirrel'). Suffixes added to the basic form take stress on every other syllable counting from that root stress (/yó-wɨ-hɨ́ʔã/ 'around the canoe', /kaʔsá-maʔ-síʔi/ 'I will not throw it', /deʔwá-ka-tó-taʔá-de/). Within a diphthong the accent falls on the second vowel (/yaí/, /saó/); across a syllable division it falls on the first (/kúa-hi/). Sec. 2.2.1 also refers to 'el acento fuerte' (the strong stress) as the condition for retaining the glottal stop.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not labelled as secondary: the grammar says only that after suffixation 'las sílabas alternas llevan el acento' (alternate syllables carry the stress) and marks all such syllables with the same acute, e.g. /yó-wɨ-hɨ́ʔã/, /hasó-síʔi/, /deʔwá-ka-tó-taʔá-de/; i.e. a rhythmic alternating pattern anchored on the root stress, with no statement of which peak is primary (the phrase 'acento fuerte' in sec. 2.2.1 implies degrees of stress but is not developed).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions. The one apparent deviation, /kúa-hi/ 'he takes him along' (stress on the first of two vowels), is explained in sec. 2.4 as a syllable division between the vowels (root /kú/ + causative /-a/), not as an exception. Sec. 2.6 notes that the tilde is normally not written in the practical orthography because Secoyas 'lo pueden deducir correctamente por el contexto gramatical' (can deduce it correctly from the grammatical context), consistent with stress being predictable from the root.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1990 grammar describes the Ecuadorian Secoya of the Aguarico river (San Pablo and Sehuayá, below the mouth of the Eno) and the Cuyabeno community (sec. 1.1); it counts the Angutero/Angotero as Secoya with only minor dialect differences, and separates the Eno-river Siona as dialectally distinct but mutually intelligible. The Rosetta Project scans are of this Quito 1990 ILV edition (title page: 'basada en un borrador elaborado por Alva Wheeler').

readall_conflicts: Within the one listed work there is no internal disagreement. For context only (not in the works list; already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 pass): Johnson & Peeke 1962 'Phonemic units in the Secoya word' (pp. 83-85) analyses the 'stress-group nucleus' as having four contrastive stress patterns (single stress, stress-stress, stress-nonstress, nonstress-stress) over one or two syllables, with marginal (suffixal) stress patterns 'unidentified as yet'; that earlier analysis treats root stress as contrastive rather than fixed on the second syllable, so it differs in type from the 1990 grammar's statement. The 1990 grammar (co-authored by Johnson) supersedes it as the reference description and is the source of the second-syllable rule.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation was confirmed verbatim on PDF pp. 6-7 (sec. 2.3) of the Rosetta scan we hold of Johnson & Levinsohn 1990. (2) That work is the only reference grammar of Secoya in Glottolog's 66-item bibliography and no later stress/prosody study was found (Vallejos 2013, held, treats segmental phonology and tone only). (3) I downloaded the 1962 SIL precursor article (Johnson & Peeke) from an Internet Archive copy and scanned it: it already ties margin (suffix) stress to morphological structure and treats stem stress patterns as distribution classes of the word nucleus, including a stress-nonstress disyllabic type (ɨ́mɨ, yówɨ) that the 1990 grammar reanalyses as monosyllabic root + suffix (yó-wɨ).
